OpenAI Countersues Apple And Accuses It Of Stealing Trade Secrets
The suit suggests that the iPhone maker is trying to “compete unfairly by any means available.” Unsplash/Solen Feyissa Add Engadget on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover OpenAI has filed a major lawsuit against Apple that accuses the iPhone maker of stealing trade secrets, according to a report by Financial Times . The folks behind ChatGPT have also accused Apple of "coercing and threatening" suppliers who work with both companies. OpenAI says Apple is trying to "compete unfairly by any means available", which includes encouraging employees to store corporate files on personal devices and cloud storage accounts. The complaint is filled with flowery language that suggests "Apple set quite a trap for employees" and that "bright young minds thought they would work in Cupertino. Instead they were joining Hotel California: you can check out any time you like, but you can never leave." This follows a suit issued by Apple against OpenAI that accused the AI company of stealing secret trade information . This was filed after OpenAI acquired an entity called io , which is a studio led by Apple's former design chief Jony Ive. At that point, Apple called ChatGPT "rotten to its core." Now it looks like OpenAI is getting involved in a bit of tit for tat. Apple has yet to comment on today's lawsuit, but it wasn't that long ago in which the two companies were partnered up to bring ChatGPT to iPhones . Now OpenAI is prepping its own line of hardware products that could directly compete with Apple. To that end, the company has accused a former employee of returning to Apple and sharing details about product plans and suppliers . This is pretty much the exact same thing Apple accused OpenAI of doing in its suit. That filing names several former Apple employees and says they "surreptitiously accessed and downloaded dozens of Apple's confidential hardware-related files, including voluminous, detailed information about unreleased products, engineering presentations, technical specifications and proprietary project data." In any event, the courts will have to settle this whole thing. We'll keep you posted as these two suits make their way through the legal system.

articles.title: OpenAI vs Apple: What is the trade secrets dispute, and why are the two tech giants heading for a legal battle?
articles.text:
OpenAI vs Apple: What is the trade secrets dispute, and why are the two tech giants heading for a legal battle? | Company Business News OpenAI vs Apple: What is the trade secrets dispute, and why are the two tech giants heading for a legal battle? ( Reuters ) AI Quick Read OpenAI has countersued Apple, accusing the iPhone maker of stealing its trade secrets, pressuring shared suppliers to limit their work with the artificial intelligence company and using restrictive employment agreements to prevent employees from joining competitors. The counterclaims, filed on Friday in a federal court in San Jose, California, escalate an ongoing legal battle between the two companies, which had partnered to integrate ChatGPT into Apple's devices in 2024. According to Bloomberg , OpenAI alleged that Apple was using its influence over suppliers and engineers to undermine its entry into the hardware market. The AI company is developing a range of connected devices with former Apple design chief Jony Ive, with a smart speaker expected to be among its first products. In its filing, OpenAI claimed that Apple was demanding that suppliers disclose their projects for the AI company, along with the names and assignments of employees working on them. "Suppliers have expressed fear of losing Apple business and have moved or rescheduled meetings with OpenAI to avoid Apple seeing them," OpenAI said in its counterclaims, according to AFP . The company also alleged that one supplier shifted manufacturing work for its products to the night shift to avoid overlapping with its Apple projects, increasing costs. Another supplier allegedly abandoned planned work following pressure from Apple. OpenAI has also accused a former employee, who left the company in June and returned to Apple, of taking confidential information about its unreleased hardware. According to the counterclaims, the former employee sent a large number of OpenAI documents, including information about a prototype, to personal accounts before presenting the company's hardware plans to senior Apple executives. OpenAI alleged that the presentation took place at Apple's request. The AI company has also challenged Apple's employment agreements, arguing that provisions preventing former employees from recruiting their previous colleagues for a year restrict employee mobility and make it harder for OpenAI to hire engineers. It further argued that Apple's intellectual property agreements define confidential information too broadly, potentially restricting employees from using professional skills and knowledge gained during their careers. The counterclaims are part of a lawsuit Apple filed in July against OpenAI and two former Apple employees, including Chang Liu, who joined the AI company in January. Apple accused OpenAI employees of deliberately accessing and using confidential information about its unreleased products and technologies. The iPhone maker alleged that Liu accessed confidential hardware-related files over several weeks after exploiting an authentication vulnerability in Apple's shared network. It also claimed that OpenAI approached Apple employees for jobs and asked some candidates to bring actual Apple hardware components to interviews. Apple has rejected OpenAI's latest allegations, calling the counterclaims a "transparent attempt to distract from the substance" of its lawsuit. The company said its case concerned the deliberate theft and use of confidential information relating to unreleased technologies, processes and products, rather than the inadvertent retention of information. Apple also said it had policies to prevent employees from using confidential information belonging to former employers and had found no evidence supporting OpenAI's allegations. Livestream Menu In this article OpenAI sued Apple on Friday, accusing the Big Tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices, after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology. The ChatGPT maker filed counterclaims in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple's employment practices were designed to "trap" employees and prevent them from working on competitors' technology. OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal electronic devices that threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf," the company said in its Friday court filing. OpenAI said in the filing that Apple gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who worked at OpenAI for six months. In that time, the employee gained access to specific information on a new device as well as OpenAI's roadmap for future hardware products. "Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place," OpenAI said. Apple denied using the rehired employee to access OpenAI's confidential information and denied trying to suppress competition in AI device manufacturing. "OpenAI's counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple's lawsuit," Apple said in a Friday statement. Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as the intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition for talent and proprietary technology. Apple sued OpenAI and former Apple employees Tang Tan and Chang Liu in July, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner's foray into consumer hardware. Tan, a 24-year Apple employee who was a vice president of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch, was part of the group that launched the AI device startup io Products before it was acquired by OpenAI in 2025. OpenAI and the employees have denied those allegations and said that Apple's lawsuit depended on its unauthorized monitoring of Liu's personal messages after he stopped working for Apple. OpenAI and attorneys for Tan and Liu did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday's court filing. In Friday's filing, OpenAI criticized Apple for encouraging employees to do work on their personal Apple devices and accounts, then preventing those employees from an orderly separation of work and personal accounts when they leave for new jobs. OpenAI said that Apple continues to access former employees' personal devices and accounts after they leave the company, enabling Apple to "monitor and ensnare departing employees" when they leave for competitors. OpenAI said that 400 employees have left Apple for OpenAI so far, and Apple wants to intimidate other employees from leaving to find other tech companies.

Commerce secretary asks exporters to leverage FTAs, build supply chains | Economy & Policy News - Business Standard
Rajesh Agrawal, Commerce secretary Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal has asked exporters to identify sector-specific opportunities in countries with which India has implemented free trade agreements (FTAs) and develop overseas supply chains to boost exports. Agrawal said that FTAs provide huge opportunities for exporters, particularly Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs). India has implemented trade pacts with countries including Oman, the UK, New Zealand, Australia, and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) bloc. India's preferential access to global markets, representing around $10 trillion in GDP until a few years ago, had expanded by an additional $60 trillion over the last four-and-a-half years through these FTAs, taking the total to about $70 trillion. With ongoing bilateral and multilateral trade engagements across eight to nine geographies, this was expected to expand to around $85 trillion, representing nearly 76 per cent of global GDP, over the next year to year-and-a-half. The commerce ministry is organising a series of workshops to spread awareness about opportunities being provided by these pacts. "He encouraged exporters to identify sector-specific opportunities in FTA partner countries, participate in international exhibitions, develop overseas supply chains and explore emerging avenues such as cross-border e-commerce," the ministry said. The secretary was speaking at an outreach initiative in Jaipur on November 27. It was organised to familiarise exporters, entrepreneurs and Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) with opportunities arising from India's Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and facilitate greater access to international markets. Norse Atlantic Airways operated low-cost, long-haul flights around the world, including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia. Photograph: Reuters Norse Atlantic Airways files for bankruptcy and cancels all future flights Norwegian airline tells customers not to come to airports after surging fuel costs caused by Iran war ruin finances Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances. The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical. The carrier operated low-cost, long-haul flights around the world, including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia. Flights from Gatwick and Manchester next month to Thailand are among those now scrapped, along with London flights to South Africa and the US. The Norse board concluded operations were no longer viable after a year in which airlines across the world were hit by spiralling oil prices that doubled the cost of jet fuel as well as dampening consumer demand, after the Iran war began in February. Rival airlines have predicted surging air fares and the collapse of weaker carriers . In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Eivind Roald, the chief executive of Norse, said: “The board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution. “We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners.” He said the owning group and Norse’s UK subsidiary – which was set up to comply with aviation rules after Brexit – were “working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations”. However, all UK flights were similarly cancelled and ticket sales halted. In a message on its website, Norse advised passengers to contact their travel agents, flight bookers, insurers or credit card companies, but made clear those travelling were on their own and should ask airport information desks. It said: “We know this will disrupt travel plans and may leave some passengers away from home. Customer service for both airlines is no longer available by phone, email, chat or social media.” after newsletter promotion The abrupt end came after Norse announced it was on the brink of collapse on Thursday morning. On Friday morning, it reported that aircraft lessors had served termination notices for the 12 planes in its fleet. Norse was founded in 2021, attempting to emulate the model of Norwegian Air , whose attempts to forge a new low-cost long-haul market ended with the pandemic. Norse briefly revived the transatlantic routes using the same plane types, Boeing 787 Dreamliners. However, it eventually hit similar financial turbulence and this summer told investors it was exploring a sale or merger, embarking on a $50m (£38m) cost-cutting programme, including shedding jobs and its Norwegian HQ.

articles.text:
Norse Atlantic Airways files for bankruptcy after failing to secure funding
Livestream Menu In this article Budget carrier Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy Friday, saying it failed to secure funding after soaring fuel costs strained the company's operations throughout the year. Its parent company, Norse Atlantic ASA, concluded that the Norwegian carrier no longer has a basis to continue operations. "Despite extensive efforts, the Company has so far not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs," the firm said in a statement Friday. It comes days after Norse said it's facing a "critical financial situation" and was considering its options from a strategic takeover to ACMI contracts, which refer to short-term capacity leasing. The company's shares closed 85% lower on Wednesday. The board has now filed a bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court, where a trustee will be appointed to manage the process further. "The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the Company and the Group to find a solution," Norse Atlantic CEO Eivind Roald said. "We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners. The Board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald added. The company has canceled all flights, and ticket sales have been discontinued. Norse was founded in March 2021 and offered cheap flights between Europe, North America, Africa and Asia. The Iran war began on Feb. 28 and caused jet fuel prices to skyrocket, forcing airlines around the world to grapple with higher costs. Prices are now up nearly 72% to $155 per barrel year-on-year as of the week ending Nov. 20, according to the International Air Transport Association's Jet Fuel Price Monitor . Norse Atlantic's Roald told CNBC in May that he wasn't "overly concerned" about access to fuel but flagged that the company had canceled over 700 flights, which impacted more than 240,000 passengers. Ryanair's CEO Michael O'Leary warned in April that if jet fuel prices continued to stay elevated throughout the year, then other European airlines were likely to face "financial difficulties" during the winter season. In fact, several European airlines have stopped operating this winter, including Slovakia's AirExplore, Spain's AlbaStar, Ireland's Fly4 and Spain's Plus Ultra, which has canceled all flights but hasn't permanently closed.

articles.title: German software firm SAP is reportedly cutting at least 10,000 jobs in AI push
articles.text:
SAP weighs cutting at least 10,000 jobs in AI push: Bloomberg
Livestream Menu In this article SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as the German firm reshapes its software business for the artificial intelligence era, Bloomberg reported on Thursday , citing people familiar with the matter. "The business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful," SAP said in a statement to CNBC. "As part of this ongoing transformation, roles and functions will naturally change over time. Beyond this, no decisions have been made regarding any further measures. We do not comment on speculation." The company did not provide any further details on potential job cuts. The report came as the company flagged a cybersecurity attack, but said it had found "no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data." "SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services," a company spokesperson said. "Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on." Other software companies have also tied workforce reductions to AI initiatives, though for different reasons. WiseTech Global said in February it planned to cut about 2,000 jobs over two years as it integrated AI into its products and operations. Atlassian said in March it would cut about 1,600 jobs partly to fund further AI investment, while Cloudflare said in May it would eliminate more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model. In the U.S., employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, accounting for about 20% of the total, according to a Nov. 5 report from outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide. Bloomberg reported that all departments had been asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales in particular focus. The company also underwent a reorganization in 2024, when it eliminated around 10,000 positions through a program that relied mainly on voluntary departures and retraining. Its headcount later remained relatively flat as it hired for new roles, Bloomberg reported. In 2023, SAP CEO Christian Klein told CNBC he did not necessarily expect a reduction in the workforce, saying he expected the company to grow and "accelerate" its total revenue. The reported cuts come as Klein pushes SAP toward an AI-first strategy . This year, SAP completed four acquisitions — Reltio, Dremio, Prior Labs and TechWolf — and made strategic investments in AI-focused companies including Parloa, n8n and Conduct. The acquisitions are intended to help SAP organize company data, develop AI models for business information and analyze workforce skills.

Bisleri's 20-cent bottles have made the ‌company a household name in India, where poor water quality has ​turned bottled water into a necessity for homes and ​restaurants. It has remained the market leader while competing with PepsiCo and Coca-Cola in India's $3.5 billion packaged drinking-water market. Consumer worries were already heightened ​in India after the food regulator said this week it had found a sample of Bisleri water unsafe due to the presence of chemicals that health agencies say may cause cancer. In the second notice to Bisleri, dated August 12 and seen by Reuters, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India relayed its findings to the company and asked it to prohibit the sale of the affected batch citing ​the presence of bacteria. "The sample was found to be non-conforming (UNSAFE)," the notice said. "It shows presence of coliform." Bisleri says independent ​testing shows no problem Bisleri says it has 130 operational plants making its products and 5,980 distributors. Multinational conglomerate Tata was previously in talks to acquire the bottler, which counts several Bollywood stars among brand ambassadors, including Deepika Padukone. Mumbai-based Bisleri told Reuters in a statement on Saturday that it had recalled the batch ‌in August on the government's instructions and that "the primary and ​referral laboratories reported the presence of coliform bacteria in the ‌regulatory sample". But the company said it commissioned independent testing of samples from the same batch, which found they met "the applicable standard for coliform ‌bacteria ??and all other applicable food safety standards". "The difference between the regulatory and independent findings warrants a thorough review," the company said. "Bisleri will continue ​to cooperate fully with FSSAI to establish the facts." The regulator did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Reuters reported on Monday that the food regulator had asked all states to strengthen oversight and intensify surveillance ​of the packaged water industry in light of the Bisleri findings. The agency ordered states to hold "regular inspections and risk-based sampling of packaged drinking water and mineral water", saying "appropriate action shall be initiated in cases of non-compliance". The checks will increase ‌regulatory oversight of PepsiCo, Tata Consumer, Coca-Cola and billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Consumer, which have all bet on the sector. In the first finding ‌against Bisleri, court records show that the food regulator has initiated prosecution proceedings, which could include a jail term and fine for manufacturing a sample found unsafe. Indian authorities have stepped up enforcement against major food and drinks brands in recent weeks. Federal and state regulators have conducted many raids and reprimanded companies for improper labelling, affecting everyone from Domino's to Diageo. FSSAI sanctions prosecution against Bisleri over bacteria-positive sample This is Bisleri’s second sanctions of prosecution after a Goa plant sample failed testing, following Sunday’s similar action by the regulator By Meenakshi Verma Ambwani Updated - November 28, 2026 at 12:51 PM. | New Delhi × Share WhatsApp X Facebook LinkedIn Messenger Reddit Mail https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/companies/fssai-sanctions-prosecution-against-bisleri-over-bacteria-positive-sample/article71753820.ece Copy The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International after finding a sample of its packaged drinking water “unsafe” due to presence of coliform bacteria, which was confirmed during both primary and referral lab testing, sources said. The regulator had also prohibited the sale of one specific batch of packaged drinking water manufactured in its plant in West Bengal on August 12, marking the second instance of regulatory action against Bisleri in recent days. Bisleri said it has already recalled that particular batch at the direction of the regulator and has sought review of the test results. This is the second instance of sanction of prosecution against Bisleri after a sample collected from one of its plants in Goa also failed testing parameters. This also comes at a time when the regulator has directed states to step up surveillance and enforcement drives in the packaged drinking water segment. Sources said that one regulatory sample of Bisleri packaged drinking water lifted from the company’s facility in Telipara, Jalpaiguri district, West Bengal, was found unsafe due to the presence of coliform bacteria. Sources added that the presence of coliform bacteria was confirmed by both primary and referral labs, which resulted in the prohibition of sale order against one batch (Batch No. PB 201) being issued, besides sanction for prosecution also been issued against the company. In a statement, Bisleri International Pvt Ltd said it had already recalled Batch PB201 of its packaged drinking water at the direction of FSSAI. “The primary and referral laboratories reported the presence of coliform bacteria in the regulatory sample. Bisleri separately commissioned independent testing of samples from the same batch at an FSSAI-recognised laboratory, which found that the sample met the applicable standard for coliform bacteria and all other applicable food safety standards,” the company added. It said that it also had samples tested at another independent, FSSAI-recognised laboratory which also reported that the sample met the applicable standard for coliform bacteria. “The difference between the regulatory and independent findings warrants a thorough review. Bisleri calls upon FSSAI to examine the sampling process, testing methodology, laboratory findings and any factors that may have contributed to the variation in results. We expect this matter to be assessed against the same standards applied across the industry. Bisleri will continue to cooperate fully with FSSAI to establish the facts,” the company’s statement added. Official sources said that packaged drinking and mineral water samples of other brands have also been lifted and their facilities have also been inspected. Recently, FSSAI has also directed State food safety commissioners and regional directors to direct food safety officers in their jurisdictions to conduct regular inspections and risk-based sampling of packaged drinking water and mineral water brands.
